I dunno if any of us are wrong or right, but there have been several times in the past when we, as a society, were told that "this new technology will make everything so much easier and you'll have tons of leisure time."

First example, the automobile. Automobiles were going to shorten our commutes and journeys and so, leaving our workplace or making a journey at 3pm would have us arriving at 3:30pm with tons of leisure and no fatigue, compared to arriving at 6pm and tired. The reality was that we simply worked longer or allocated more activity since travel took less time.

Second example, the computer. We were told that computers were going to make everything easier and we would complete all of our work in half of the time, again, thereby allowing us tons of leisure time. Again, we were simply given double the work (which in aggregate, was a good thing because it got us to this conversation in half the time).

So, I would propose that the road ahead does not lead to some utopia, but rather to some difficulty that is outside of our frame of understand/cultural bias.

But I'm just a gamer, so meh.

comments.author: @tomaalimosh
comments.text: The only thing I disaggree with here is the leverage point. The balance of power right now is maintained by some implicit assumptions. One of those assumptions is that if the "ruling" class doesn't prioritise the needs of the "working" class, they could theoretically retaliate by withholding their labor or even revolting. so you reach some kind of Nash equilibrium. If human labor is no longer needed, and there is no more strength in numbers for a potential revolt, then there is no way the vast majority of people can retaliate to any potential deterioration of their living conditions. This means that even if their standard of living may significantly improve initially, there is nothing preventing it from going all the way down (for all kinds of different reasons - malice, sociopathic manifestations of power over other humans, or even indifference). The Nash equilibrium for a game where one player has 0 power is 0.

Suppose we aim for a steady-state economy post Ai - no change in demand (ability to pay - maybe everyone gets a UBI), no change in total production, manufacturers get to keep making just as much profit as now (say 5% of current prices).
After all labor costs are gone, manufacturers' costs of capital equipment and input materials also start to fall because the suppliers of those things are also able to reduce their prices while maintaining their profit... 
Cost reductions cascade through the supply chains, until eventually prices of goods level out around  ~15% of current prices.
So if we took the total of all wages currently paid (around $11T) then subtract out income taxes (leaving just spendable wage income), and distributed 15% of that total (around $1.3T - about as much as is spent on social security) evenly to everyone as a tax-free UBI of about $4000/yr once no one is working, our economy would be mostly unchanged. 
Of course, since it is distributed evenly, there would be some shifts in consumption, but this is a decent first approximation.
The rich would also see prices fall to 85%, so they'd effectively be about 7x more wealthy, while the rest of us only get 3.5x as many days off.

comments.text: The flaw in the premise is that substituting human resource by AI resource reduces business costs to nil or the point where humans have no value. This will simply not be the case - e.g. electricity, computers are still required for AI, which draw on limited or constrained resources to be provisioned. The value of those constrained resources (especially natural resources) will therefore increase due to demand, increasing the cost of deploying AI. AI reduces the scarcity of labour resource, and therefore its value. So the value of humans will fall to match AI costs, and consequentially human purchasing power will also initially fall, but as a result so will the price of outputs from companies. Afterall, how will companies make money if no one is able to purchase their goods or services - selling AI outputs to another AI makes no sense unless the cost of providing AI is cheaper than obtaining it. Instead, what we will see is a rebalance of value towards remaining constrained, natural resources.

comments.text: Has anyone ever addressed the issue from the perspective of comparative advantages? The classic example is: the Chinese will never be able to produce everything at a lower cost than us; it's a logical impossibility. Suppose there are only two goods: potatoes and carrots. Potatoes sell for $10 per kilogram, and carrots for $20 per kilogram. But if you produce carrots, you necessarily cannot produce potatoes, and viceversa. So, what will the Chinese produce? They will decide to produce only carrots. Because if they produced potatoes, they would lose money. Therefore, they cannot produce potatoes: and we will. We will never be left without work or income. What does this have to do with AI? It's the same reasoning. If you have an AI model, if you make it do something, you give up having it do something else_. So, you will decide to have it do _only the thing that has the highest market value. Therefore, they necessarily cannot do everything. There will always be something they cannot do (because if they did it, they would give up doing something else of greater value). So, there will always be something left for humans to do.
